strengths: The benchmark addresses a useful gap: precise, structure-grounded molecular recognition, editing, and generation, with exact correctness criteria rather than ambiguous property-based descriptions.
The core annotation pipeline includes peer refinement and independent reconstruction by two validators. The 18 recognition tasks cover topology, functional groups, and stereochemistry.
Evaluation spans numerous language models and image modalities, revealing substantial differences between counting and localization, and between valid SMILES generation and structural correctness.
The appendices provide model snapshots, chemistry-specific baselines, repeated o3 evaluations, SMILES enumeration experiments, prompt variations, and category-level editing results.
weaknesses: Visible example errors undermine the central claim of accurate, unambiguous ground truth. In Figure S7(c), the supplied starting SMILES contains a five-membered carbocycle, whereas the starting image and instruction specify contracting a six-membered ring to five members. In Figure S5(c), the description specifies a chlorinated indole derivative, but the labeled ground-truth image shows a different, fluorinated piperazine-containing molecule. These may be presentation errors, but an independent dataset audit is needed to establish whether evaluation instances are affected.

Results are internally inconsistent. GPT Image 1 editing accuracy is 13.5% in the introduction and Table S7, versus 8% in Table 2 and the manual audit. DeepSeek-R1 quaternary-carbon results differ between Tables 1 and S6. The claim that all models except GPT-5 perform below chance on E/Z recognition contradicts GPT-4.1's 67% in Table S6 and the image-model results.

The evaluation does not adequately separate molecular understanding from representation handling. Recognition requires manual atom enumeration, yet there is no atom-mapped SMILES or explicit connectivity baseline. The tokenization explanation relies on one illustrative error rather than a controlled intervention. Tool-assisted LLM baselines using RDKit, and image-to-SMILES-to-tool pipelines, would clarify the practical significance of the observed failures.

The annotation procedure is promising but insufficiently audited: initial agreement rates, rejection and revision frequencies, and residual error estimates are absent. Human simplicity claims lack an independent human performance baseline; agreement after iterative correction does not establish first-attempt difficulty or guarantee uniqueness.

Coverage and statistical support are limited for some conclusions. Editing and generation each have only 200 core examples, with categories such as tautomerization, charge changes, and relocation represented by only one to three examples. Five repeated model runs quantify sampling variability but do not establish uncertainty from benchmark composition. Molecular diversity, scaffold overlap, and performance by structural complexity are not sufficiently characterized.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the supplied snapshots and prompt examples. The manuscript does not precisely specify structural-equivalence normalization, including tautomerism and unspecified stereochemistry, or inference settings such as reasoning effort and token limits. These choices can materially affect exact-match results and comparisons.

strengths: The benchmark targets a useful gap: precise, structure-grounded molecular recognition, editing, and generation, rather than descriptions that admit many valid molecules.

The core editing and generation sets use a substantial annotation process involving peer review and independent reconstruction by two validators. Recognition covers 18 tasks with programmatically generated labels.

Evaluation includes numerous general-purpose models, chemistry-specific editing baselines, and image-based models. The appendix adds repeated-run measurements, SMILES enumeration tests, prompt variations, and editing-category breakdowns.
weaknesses: Concrete inconsistencies undermine the central claim of reliable, unambiguous ground truth. In Figure S7(c), the supplied SMILES already contains a five-membered saturated ring, whereas the input drawing and instruction specify contracting a six-membered ring. In Figure S5(c), the description specifies a chlorinated indole derivative, but the displayed ground-truth molecule is an unrelated fluorinated structure containing piperazine. These may be presentation errors, but the paper needs a dataset audit establishing that they do not affect evaluation.

Reported results are internally inconsistent. GPT Image 1 editing accuracy is 13.5% in the introduction and Table S7, versus 8% in Table 2 and the manual evaluation of 16/200 cases. DeepSeek-R1 quaternary-carbon performance is 0.780/0.680 in Table 1 but 0.440/0.330 in Table S6. The claim that every model except GPT-5 performs below chance on E/Z classification contradicts GPT-4.1's 67.0% in Table S6.

The evaluation does not adequately separate chemical understanding from serialization and bookkeeping. SMILES recognition requires models to enumerate atoms, whereas images provide explicit indices. Despite attributing localization errors to tokenization, the paper offers only an illustrative example, without atom-mapped SMILES, explicit connectivity inputs, or tool-assisted controls. The results establish difficulty under the chosen interface, but do not isolate the claimed reasoning limitations.

Dataset quality and human difficulty are insufficiently quantified. Validators can revise failed reconstructions, and unsuccessful examples are discarded, but initial agreement, rejection rates, and an independent human accuracy baseline are not reported. Successful reconstruction after curation does not establish that the tasks are trivial for humans or that residual ambiguity is negligible.

Coverage remains limited for the comprehensive framing. Each core editing/generation set has only 200 instances; some editing categories contain one to three examples. Graph inputs are not evaluated, and chemistry-specific models are evaluated quantitatively only on editing. The sizable generation difference between core and extended sets—43% versus 59% for GPT-5—also warrants analysis of distribution and annotation differences.

Reproducibility and interpretation need strengthening. Model snapshots are supplied, but inference budgets, reasoning settings, and exact structural-equivalence rules are insufficiently specified. The paper should clarify treatment of stereochemistry, tautomerism, and alternative valid representations. Better performance by newer models is not independent evidence of annotation correctness. Overall, the promising benchmark concept does not overcome the unresolved data-quality and evaluation issues.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a useful gap: precise, structure-grounded recognition, editing, and generation, with explicit atom localization and exact molecular correctness rather than ambiguous property-based descriptions.

The collection effort is substantial: 18 recognition tasks, 200 core examples each for editing and generation, additional extended sets, and a multi-stage expert annotation and reconstruction protocol.

Evaluation covers numerous general-purpose and reasoning models, chemistry-specific baselines, and image modalities. Separating validity from correctness reveals meaningful failures that validity alone would miss.
The appendix provides useful checks involving repeated runs, SMILES enumeration, instruction paraphrasing, and performance by editing category.
weaknesses: Visible example inconsistencies undermine the central claim of rigorously verified ground truth. In Figure S7(c), the supplied starting SMILES contains a five-membered saturated ring, whereas the image and instruction specify contracting a six-membered ring to five. In Figure S5(c), the description specifies a chlorinated indole-based structure, but the displayed ground truth instead contains a fluorinated, piperazine-containing structure. These could be presentation errors, but an audit is needed to establish that evaluated examples are unaffected.

Results contain material inconsistencies. GPT Image 1 editing accuracy is 13.5% in the introduction and Table S7, but 8% in Table 2 and the manual evaluation in A.10. DeepSeek-R1 quaternary-carbon performance is 0.780/0.680 in Table 1 versus 0.440/0.330 in Table S6. The claim that every model except GPT-5 performs below chance on E/Z classification contradicts GPT-4.1's 67% in Table S6.

The evaluation does not sufficiently separate molecular understanding from representation and output difficulties. Atom enumeration is required for SMILES inputs but supplied for images; there is no indexed-SMILES control, tool-assisted baseline, or image-to-SMILES-plus-reasoning baseline. The proposed tokenization explanation remains speculative without a controlled intervention.

Dataset reliability and coverage need stronger quantitative support. Validator reconstruction is part of sample selection, rather than an independent held-out human baseline; initial agreement, rejection rates, and residual error estimates are absent. Some editing categories contain only one to three core examples. Five repeated model runs measure completion variability but do not establish uncertainty from the small evaluation samples.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite reporting model snapshots: decoding settings, reasoning budgets, output limits, and precise structural-equivalence rules are not specified adequately. Choosing canonical SMILES versus InChI-based comparison can matter for tautomerization and stereochemistry, both relevant to this benchmark.

The resource has promise, but its broad claims about human simplicity, annotation quality inferred from model rankings, and general molecular reasoning limitations exceed the evidence. Given that trustworthy exact evaluation is the principal contribution, the unresolved ground-truth and reporting issues prevent acceptance at a selective venue.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a useful gap: precise, structure-grounded language tasks with exact molecular targets, complementing datasets whose descriptions mix structural and functional information.

The core annotation pipeline includes peer refinement and independent reconstruction by two validators. Annotation guidelines, rejection statistics, and category breakdowns provide useful transparency.

Evaluation covers numerous general-purpose, chemistry-specific, graph-language, and visual models. Additional experiments examine SMILES enumeration, paraphrasing, SELFIES, repeated runs, and pass@k, while error analyses identify concrete challenges in stereochemistry and molecular topology.
weaknesses: Visible inconsistencies undermine the central claim of accurate, unambiguous ground truth. In Figure S11(c), the supplied SMILES already contains a five-membered ring, whereas the image and instruction specify contracting a six-membered ring to five. Figure S9(c) describes a chlorinated indole derivative but shows an unrelated fluorinated structure as ground truth. Figure S8(d) describes a benzene ring as disubstituted with ethoxy groups while the reference has one ethoxy group and a different oxygen-linked chain, making the purported extra-substructure error questionable. These may include presentation mistakes, but an independent dataset audit is needed to establish whether reported model errors reflect incorrect predictions or inconsistent references.

The experiments conflate molecular understanding with representation handling and output-format compliance. There is no atom-indexed SMILES or explicit adjacency-list control to isolate enumeration errors, and no tool-assisted baseline using cheminformatics parsing or constrained molecular output. The tokenization explanation rests primarily on an illustrative example. Poor zero-shot performance therefore supports a narrower conclusion than the claimed fundamental limitations of chemical reasoning.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the model snapshot table and prompt examples. The manuscript does not specify decoding settings, reasoning budgets, output limits, or the precise structural-equivalence implementation, including treatment of stereochemistry, aromaticity, charges, and tautomers. These choices materially affect an exact-match benchmark.

Coverage and statistical support are insufficient for some broad claims. Each core editing/generation task has only 200 examples, with some editing categories represented by one to three instances. The extended sets change both annotation procedure and category distribution, and GPT-5 generation accuracy shifts from 43% to 59% without a substantive explanation. Repeated o3 runs measure sampling variability, but do not establish uncertainty in model rankings or population coverage; a t-SNE visualization alone cannot establish representativeness.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. The downstream study compares direct prediction with structure-first prompting without a matched general-reasoning control, so it does not establish that improved structural recognition causes the gains or is necessary for downstream success. Likewise, poor instruction following by specialized models does not establish their inability to perform property or reaction prediction. Reporting also needs reconciliation: the introduction gives GPT Image 1 editing accuracy as 13.5%, whereas Table 2 and Appendix A.17 report 8%.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a useful gap: precise structure-grounded recognition, editing, and reconstruction, with separate recognition and atom-localization metrics.
The annotation workflow includes peer review and independent reconstruction by two validators. Annotation-round statistics and rejection counts provide useful transparency.

The evaluation is substantial, covering general-purpose, chemistry-specific, graph-language, and image models. The appendix adds repeated runs, pass@k, SMILES enumeration, paraphrasing, SELFIES comparisons, and qualitative error analysis.
weaknesses: Published examples undermine the central claim of unambiguous, correct ground truth. Figure S9(c) describes a chlorinated indole, but the reference drawing shows a different, fluorinated molecule containing a piperazine ring. In Figure S11(c), the supplied SMILES contains a five-membered ring, while the starting drawing and instruction specify contraction of a six-membered ring. Figure S8(d) describes a ring as 'ortho-disubstituted with ethoxy groups,' whereas the reference contains one ethoxy substituent and a distinct aminoethyl-oxy linkage. These could include presentation errors, but an independent dataset audit is needed to establish whether evaluation inputs and references are reliable.

The evaluation does not adequately separate molecular understanding from serialization and indexing difficulty. Localization requires manually enumerating SMILES atoms, and generation combines structural interpretation with producing valid SMILES. SELFIES experiments are useful but do not resolve this confound. Atom-mapped SMILES, explicit connectivity inputs, and a tool-assisted baseline would better substantiate claims about fundamental structural-reasoning limitations. The proposed BPE explanation remains speculative.

Claims of downstream necessity exceed the evidence. Appendix A.13 shows that structure-first prompting improves property-prediction accuracy for two models on two datasets, but lacks a comparable generic reasoning control and does not demonstrate that improved MolLangBench performance causes improved downstream performance. Poor zero-shot instruction following by specialized models also does not establish their inability to perform property or reaction prediction.

Several quantitative statements contradict the reported tables. GPT Image 1 editing accuracy is 13.5% in the introduction and Table S5, versus 8% in Table 2 and Appendix A.17. The statement that every model except GPT-5 performs below chance on E/Z classification conflicts with Table S4, including GPT-4.1 at 67%. The headline 86.2% recognition result is the localization average in Table 1; recognition accuracy is 92.3%. These discrepancies require reconciliation.

Dataset coverage and human difficulty are insufficiently established. Each core editing/generation set contains only 200 examples, with some edit categories represented by one to three cases. A t-SNE visualization does not establish representativeness. Claims that tasks are simple for humans lack an independent human baseline; the reported validation process required a second reconstruction for one validator on 81 of the 200 accepted generation examples.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete despite the supplied model snapshots and robustness experiments. The manuscript does not adequately specify decoding budgets, reasoning settings, or the exact molecular-equivalence procedure used for scoring. Repeated-run variability for o3 does not quantify sampling uncertainty or establish the significance of differences between leading models.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a meaningful gap: precise, structure-grounded molecular recognition, editing, and generation, rather than descriptions that conflate structure with biological properties.
The proposed curation process is substantial, including expert peer review, independent reconstruction by two validators, and reporting of annotation revisions and rejection counts.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering general-purpose, chemistry-specific, graph-language, and image models. Supplementary experiments examine SMILES enumeration, paraphrasing, SELFIES, repeated runs, and multiple-attempt accuracy.
Separating counting from atom localization and analyzing stereochemical, connectivity, and syntax errors provides useful diagnostic information.
weaknesses: The central ground-truth quality claim is undermined by concrete inconsistencies. Figure S9c describes a chlorinated indole but shows an unrelated fluorinated, piperazine-containing reference molecule. Figure S11c requests cyclohexane-to-cyclopentane contraction, but its input SMILES already contains a five-membered ring while the image shows six. Figure S8d describes a benzene ring as disubstituted with ethoxy groups, whereas the reference contains one ethoxy group and the aminoethyl-oxygen linkage. These may be presentation errors, but an independent dataset audit and corrected evaluation are needed to establish that they do not affect benchmark scores.

Headline results are inconsistently reported. GPT Image 1 editing accuracy is 13.5% in the introduction and Table S5 but 8% in Table 2 and the manual evaluation. The abstract calls 86.2% recognition accuracy, whereas Table 1 reports 92.3% recognition and 86.2% in the localization column. The aggregate metric needs an explicit definition and consistent labeling.

The experiments do not adequately separate chemical understanding from serialization and indexing difficulties. Atom-mapped SMILES, explicit graph inputs to the same LLM, and tool-assisted parsing or generation baselines would help establish this distinction. A tokenization example does not establish BPE as the cause of localization failures, and poor zero-shot instruction following by specialist models does not establish inability on their intended downstream tasks.

Coverage and statistical support remain limited for some conclusions. Core editing and generation sets contain only 200 examples each, with several editing categories represented by one to three instances. Run-to-run variance for o3 does not quantify uncertainty from dataset sampling or establish significant differences between leading models. A t-SNE visualization also does not establish representativeness, and validator agreement after retries is not an independent human performance baseline.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite useful model snapshots and prompt examples: decoding settings, reasoning budgets, exact structural-equivalence rules, and fingerprint settings require specification. The property-prediction experiment also lacks a matched generic-reasoning control, so its gains do not establish that structure recognition is a necessary prerequisite for downstream success.
